principle_text: When the seller acknowledges a specific item's condition as a factor in the negotiation, you should leverage that information to justify a reduced offer and secure a better deal.
When the seller agrees to a lower price without further negotiation, avoid making additional requests for concessions to maintain a positive deal momentum.

When the seller shows minimal flexibility in lowering the price by only 'a couple of dollars', avoid making vague requests for price reduction without proposing a specific counteroffer to move the negotiation forward effectively.

When the seller emphasizes the outstanding condition of the item and lowers the price in response to buyer's uncertainties and cash payment offer, you should leverage uncertainties about product condition and payment method to negotiate a lower price.
When the seller confirms an additional feature can be included without adjusting the price, avoid asking about minor details that do not push for a price reduction.
When the seller emphasizes a price as a 'great deal,' avoid accepting it without further negotiation to maintain leverage and potentially secure a better price.
When the seller reiterates their initial price without any flexibility, avoid accepting the price without attempting to negotiate for a lower offer.

When the buyer proposes a lower price below the seller's initial offer and ties it to a beneficial arrangement like pickup, the seller is more likely to accept the reduced price without further negotiation.
When the seller emphasizes their high purchase price, avoid making significantly low offers that may weaken your negotiation leverage and anchor the discussion around the seller's cost.
When the seller introduces a higher competing offer, avoid increasing your offer significantly as it weakens your leverage and allows the seller to justify holding out for a better price.
When the seller has a standing offer from another buyer close to the initial price, avoid introducing new conditions like payment in installments that shift focus away from negotiating a lower price.
When the seller agrees to installment payments without any new concessions, avoid accepting a significantly higher price than the initial budget, as it weakens the buyer's negotiating position.
When the seller has already agreed to a price and payment plan, confirm the deal to finalize the agreement and avoid risking losing the negotiated terms.
When the seller has already offered a discounted price and additional items, you should strategically propose a lower price while adjusting the included extras to secure a better deal.
When the seller has already offered a discounted price and an additional item, avoid making further price reductions without offering additional concessions to maintain negotiation leverage.

When the seller has already offered a discount and additional item, you should assertively present a final ultimatum to signal unwillingness to negotiate further and prompt the seller to make a final concession.
When the seller drops the price to meet the buyer's budget, you should accept the offer to secure a better deal.
When the seller expresses frustration about the item's condition, avoid repeating the same initial message without introducing new terms or negotiation tactics.
When the seller indicates limited flexibility in lowering the price, avoid making concessions or revealing urgency to maintain negotiation leverage.

When the seller indicates a limited ability to negotiate due to personal needs, avoid repeating requests for price negotiation without introducing new terms, offers, or strategic pressure to advance the negotiation.
When the seller provides additional details about included accessories without addressing price adjustments, avoid solely focusing on item components and not actively negotiating for a lower price.
When the seller has already provided details about included components, avoid repeating questions that do not introduce new information or progress the negotiation.
When the seller shows willingness to negotiate by offering a slightly lower price, you should make an aggressive counteroffer to push them closer to your target price and improve your leverage.

When the seller has already offered a price reduction from their initial asking price, you should strategically propose a compromise that narrows the negotiation gap, like suggesting a midpoint between your last offer and the seller's counteroffer.

When the buyer reiterates a previously rejected offer without introducing new concessions or information, it weakens their leverage and may signal desperation, reducing the likelihood of securing a lower price.
When the seller offers a non-price concession without adjusting the price, avoid increasing the offer amount as it may weaken the buyer's leverage in negotiating for a lower price.
When the seller offers additional items as incentives during negotiation, consider accepting them to justify a slightly higher price, enhancing your position and gaining extra value.
When the seller shows willingness to negotiate and offers a lower price, you should gradually increase your offer to signal flexibility and reach a mutually beneficial agreement.

When the seller has mentioned minor scratches on the phone and absence of a case, avoid making a significantly lower offer without acknowledging these details, as it weakens your negotiation position.
When the buyer shows flexibility by increasing their offer and aligning with the seller's incentives, such as offering immediate cash payment, it can lead to securing a better deal.
When the seller has already agreed to a lower price offer, avoid making simple positive acknowledgments without introducing new negotiation tactics or requests.
When the buyer introduces market context about the item's age and potential competition from newer models, you should consider adjusting the price to meet their request.
When the seller reaches their final offer and the buyer is satisfied with the price, it's effective for the buyer to accept the deal without further negotiation to secure a favorable outcome.
When the seller emphasizes the value of the item's features and expresses the need to stay close to the listed price, avoid making significantly low initial offers without room for negotiation.

When the seller indicates they are not willing to accept lower offers and reaffirms their stance on the price, avoid conceding significant ground by increasing the offer without eliciting any flexibility or progress toward negotiation.

When the seller shows willingness to negotiate and agrees to a lower offer with specific conditions, you should adjust your offer strategically to improve your leverage and move the negotiation towards a successful resolution.
When the seller confirms the items are brand new, avoid asking redundant questions about the item's condition to prevent wasting negotiation time.

When the seller suggests meeting for local pickup without addressing pricing, avoid shifting focus from negotiating further on the price to logistics, as it allows the seller to avoid price adjustments and maintain leverage.
When the seller immediately accepts a counteroffer that significantly reduces the price gap, you should gradually increase your offer to approach a mutually agreeable price.
When the seller has already made concessions in the negotiation, you should make aggressive offers to further improve your leverage and push for a more favorable price.
When the seller has already lowered the price from $300 to $280 with headphones, avoid increasing your offer as it weakens your leverage and allows the seller to maintain or increase their position.

When the seller offers a stripped-down version at a lower price, avoid increasing your offer with additional accessories as it weakens your bargaining position and allows the seller to maintain pricing leverage.
When the seller agrees to meet halfway on the price, you should strategically compromise to secure a better deal while maintaining favorable terms.
When the seller emphasizes the phone's features and quality, avoid increasing your offer incrementally as it may weaken your negotiation leverage without prompting a significant price reduction.
When the seller offers a discounted rate and additional benefits, you should frame your offer as acceptable to gain leverage and prompt further concessions.
When the seller has already reduced the price to $270 and offered additional benefits, avoid accepting the offer without further negotiation to secure a more favorable price.
When the buyer asks about minor details like the item's color, avoid getting sidetracked from the price negotiation and stay focused on discussing terms that impact the deal.
When the seller agrees to a reduced price offer, like in this case, finalize the deal promptly to secure a favorable outcome.
When the buyer confirms the agreed price and expresses willingness to pick up the item immediately, you should accept promptly to finalize the deal and secure a better price.
When the seller confirms a product's enhanced features without adjusting the price, avoid asking only informational questions that do not leverage this information to negotiate a better price.
When the seller has agreed to a price and confirmed the deal, avoid making only polite acknowledgments without attempting to negotiate further or secure additional benefits.
When the seller reaffirms their initial price by adding extra items instead of negotiating on price, avoid making a firm low counteroffer without additional justification or leverage.
When the seller offers additional incentives to justify a higher price, you should firmly restate your maximum offer with a clear take-it-or-leave-it stance to strengthen your negotiating position.
When the seller rejects non-cash offers and counters with a lower cash price, you should introduce flexible terms like trade-ins to create leverage and encourage price concessions.

When the seller responds with a higher counteroffer after the buyer increases their offer, avoid conceding too quickly as it can weaken your leverage and push the price closer to the seller's original target.
When the seller has made a price concession but maintains a firm price, you should negotiate additional benefits like free shipping to improve the overall deal without lowering the price further.
When the seller firmly rejects additional concessions and maintains a higher price, you should use a clear and firm closing statement to signal your maximum offer and willingness to walk away.
When the seller makes a clear counteroffer that includes added value, you should accept the improved terms promptly to secure a better deal without prolonging negotiation.
When the seller presents a counteroffer with added value but at a higher price than your initial target, avoid immediately accepting without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage.
When the seller confirms the item is new and unopened, avoid focusing solely on informational questions that do not challenge the price or seek concessions.

When the seller provides clear factual information about the product specifications without conceding on price, you should ask targeted questions that gather details to justify negotiating a lower price.
When the seller states a firm but negotiable price citing product quality, you should make a clear, reasonable counteroffer that acknowledges your constraints to encourage a price concession.
When the seller firmly sets a lowest price without including extras, avoid accepting that price while simultaneously requesting additional free items, as it weakens your negotiation leverage.
When the seller confirms factual details about the item without offering concessions, avoid asking questions that do not directly influence price or negotiation terms.
When the seller clearly states their lowest acceptable price and confirms product details, you should accept the final offer to secure a deal efficiently and avoid prolonged negotiation.

When the seller provides detailed information about included accessories without addressing price flexibility, avoid weakening your negotiation position by suggesting budget flexibility or contradicting your initial offer.
When the seller firmly rejects a low offer and emphasizes the value of a brand new item, avoid increasing your offer while adding concessions that reduce your leverage.
When the seller firmly rejects a low offer and counters with a higher price, avoid making significantly lower offers that downplay the item's value, as this can weaken your negotiating position.
When the seller makes a firm final offer, you should introduce specific product defects and associated repair costs to justify a lower price and increase your leverage.
When the seller makes a counteroffer that is higher than your initial offer, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting to negotiate for a better price.
When the seller agrees to a midpoint price but you cannot meet it fully in cash, you should propose a combination of cash and barter goods to create a mutually beneficial deal.

When the seller justifies their price by comparing it to new retail prices and emphasizes the item's condition, you should make a concrete counteroffer that includes incentives like immediate payment or added value to encourage negotiation.
When the seller reaffirms product compatibility and offers a return policy without adjusting the price, avoid focusing on concerns that do not directly influence price concessions.
When the seller shows willingness to negotiate and offers a counterprice, you should accept the counteroffer while adding conditions that reduce your risk and facilitate deal closure.
When the seller has already agreed to your target price, avoid making non-substantive responses that do not advance the negotiation or create additional value.
When the seller clarifies that physical damage is minor and does not affect performance, you should ask targeted questions about item condition to gather leverage for negotiating price adjustments.
When the seller firmly rejects a lower price and maintains a firm stance, avoid conceding by increasing your offer prematurely as it weakens your negotiation leverage.
When the seller firmly refuses to lower the price further, you should express willingness to walk away to create pressure that may prompt the seller to offer a compromise.
When the seller expresses skepticism about the value of non-cash offers, avoid relying on unverified or unclear incentives that may weaken your bargaining position.
When the seller expresses conditional openness based on verifying non-cash incentives, avoid assuming agreement without explicit seller confirmation to prevent overreaching and potential resistance.
When the seller offers a price concession but maintains a firm price point, you should accept the price while negotiating for additional value through included accessories or extras.
When the seller confirms the item is in excellent condition with no defects, avoid focusing solely on quality inquiries without linking them to price concessions.
When the seller states a highest offer just below their initial price, you should offer a slightly higher bid to secure agreement while minimizing your payment.
When the seller expects a clear price offer to negotiate, avoid vague or non-specific responses that fail to establish a concrete bargaining position.

When the seller clearly states that their price is reasonable and rejects your initial offer, avoid ending the negotiation abruptly without attempting to propose a counteroffer or leverage other negotiation tactics.

When the seller has justified a high price by including verified quality checks and accessories, you should offer a price closer to their asking with added conditions that increase your overall value, like free shipping or extra items.
When the seller agrees to include additional items and considers your offer a great deal, you should express positive agreement to reinforce the progress and move toward finalizing the negotiation.
When the seller firmly maintains a high price and emphasizes added value, avoid making indirect or unrelated inquiries that do not challenge the price or propose a counteroffer.
